passage:
Counsellor's note, Wednesday. Mehak, school counsellor.
Aadhya, Class 5, came in after lunch with red eyes. Her younger brother's thread ceremony is on Sunday, and 'everyone is making a fuss, new clothes, a feast, and nobody asked what I get'. She asked me, 'Why do only boys get it?' I didn't argue or defend. I said it sounded lonely to watch, and that her feeling was fair. I explained that in her family's tradition this rite is given to boys, that some families now hold a similar ceremony for girls, and that she could ask her parents about it. With her permission I called her mother at 3 pm. She hadn't realised Aadhya felt left out and said they would talk tonight.

qa.q: When is her brother's thread ceremony?
qa.a: On Sunday.

qa.q: What was Aadhya feeling when she came in after lunch?
qa.a: She felt hurt and left out, watching her younger brother get all the fuss and wondering why only boys receive the rite.

qa.q: Which of Mehak's steps were helpful?
qa.a: Listening without arguing, calling the feeling fair, explaining the tradition honestly, and calling her mother the same day with her permission.

qa.q: How might Aadhya's mother feel after Mehak's call?
qa.a: She may feel surprised and sorry she hadn't noticed, and ready to talk with Aadhya that night.

grounding: Shows a child hurt that a rite is given to her brother but not to her because of gender, and a calm adult who explains the tradition while listening to her hurt.

passage:
Saturday
Today was the family puja at Ajoba's house. Only the eldest son of each branch got to do the aarti with the big lamp, so Dada, my older brother, did it and I just stood behind. I've practised the aarti song more than him! My face got hot and I stared at the floor.
Afterwards Kaka found me sitting on the stairs. He didn't say 'stop sulking'. He sat down and said, 'It's an old family custom. I was a second son too, and I minded.' He listened to everything. Then he gave me the bell to ring at the evening aarti.
At school, Jasleen said any kid can help serve langar at her gurdwara. I wish our custom were like that. But at least Kaka listened.
Omkar

qa.q: What did Kaka give Omkar?
qa.a: The bell to ring at the evening aarti.

qa.q: What was Omkar feeling while standing behind during the aarti?
qa.a: Omkar felt hurt and left out, face hot and eyes on the floor, after practising the song more than Dada.

qa.q: What did Kaka do that a calm adult could copy?
qa.a: He sat down with Omkar, explained the custom honestly, shared his own hurt as a second son, listened fully and found a real role.

qa.q: How might Dada feel if he knew Omkar was hurt?
qa.a: Dada might feel awkward or sorry, and could offer to share the lamp or practise the song together.

grounding: Illustrates a child left out of a family rite given only to the eldest son, whose hurt is honestly felt and heard by a calm adult who explains the custom.

passage:
In the village near Udupi, the whole house was busy for Ujjwal's upanayana. Nirmala, ten, watched her younger brother sit by the fire with the priest, a new sacred thread across his chest, everyone praising him.

"Why don't I get one?" she asked Amma in the kitchen. "I know more shlokas than he does."

Amma put down the ladle and sat on the step beside her. "You do. In our family the thread has been given only to boys. That's the old custom."

"That's not fair."

"It feels unfair to you, and I understand why." Amma took her hand. "Some families now do it for girls too. We can talk to Ajja about it. And tonight you can lead the shlokas at the lamp. Nobody knows them better."

Nirmala sniffed, still upset. But at the lamp that evening, she chanted loudest.

qa.q: Who received the sacred thread?
qa.a: Her younger brother Ujjwal received a new sacred thread.

qa.q: What did Nirmala feel when she asked 'Why don't I get one?'
qa.a: Nirmala felt hurt and left out, sure she knew more shlokas than her brother yet not given the thread.

qa.q: What did Amma do that was calm and fair?
qa.a: She sat with Nirmala, explained the custom honestly, agreed it felt unfair to her, offered to raise it with Ajja, and let her lead the shlokas.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal experience the day?
qa.a: Ujjwal probably feels proud and a bit nervous, perhaps without noticing how left out his sister feels.

grounding: Shows a girl hurt that a rite is given only to her brother, and a calm parent explaining the custom while listening to her hurt.

passage:
In Jin's class in Dublin, twenty-three children were making their First Holy Communion in May, and the whole spring was about it: white dresses, suits, rehearsals in the church. Jin, eight, whose family wasn't Catholic, sat in the library with a worksheet during every rehearsal.

"Everyone's getting cake and presents," said her friend Liam, trying to be kind. "You'll just be at home."

Jin cried in the girls' toilets.

Her teacher, Ms Byrne, found her and sat on the bench outside. She listened to all of it. Then she said, "The Communion is a church ceremony for Catholic families. It isn't a reward for being good. It's just not your family's tradition. But feeling left out is real, and I'm sorry."

The next week Ms Byrne asked Jin to tell the class about her family's Lunar New Year. Liam asked the most questions.

qa.q: How many children in Jin's class were making their First Holy Communion?
qa.a: Twenty-three children were making their First Holy Communion.

qa.q: How did Jin feel after Liam's comment?
qa.a: Jin felt left out and hurt, crying in the toilets.

qa.q: How did Ms Byrne handle Jin's hurt?
qa.a: She listened fully, explained calmly that the rite belongs to Catholic families and isn't a reward, said sorry for the hurt, and gave Jin a way to share her own tradition.

qa.q: How might Liam have meant his comment?
qa.a: Liam was trying to be kind but didn't realise it would make Jin feel more left out.

grounding: Shows a child left out of a rite her classmates share, and a calm teacher explaining the tradition while listening to her hurt.

passage:
At the Khalsa school in Amritsar, the hall was ready for the Dastar Bandi ceremony: twenty boys from Class 6 would have their first turbans tied before their families. Amandeep, eleven, stood at the back with the other girls, holding the tray of prasad.

Her classmate Nitin whispered, "Why aren't you up there? You wanted to."

Amandeep's throat tightened. "It's for boys."

Bhai-ji, the Gurmat teacher, overheard. After the ceremony he found her by the door. "You looked sad. Tell me."

She told him. He listened without interrupting. "Here this ceremony has always been for boys," he said. "But many Sikh women wear a dastar too. If you want one, I'll teach you, and we can ask the principal about including girls next year."

Amandeep nodded, still hurt. But she asked him for Thursday after class.

qa.q: How many boys would have their first turbans tied?
qa.a: Twenty boys from Class 6.

qa.q: What was Amandeep feeling at the back of the hall?
qa.a: Amandeep felt hurt and left out, her throat tightening because the rite was only for boys.

qa.q: How did Bhai-ji respond to Amandeep's hurt?
qa.a: He noticed, listened without interrupting, explained the tradition honestly, and offered to teach her and ask about including girls next year.

qa.q: What might Nitin have felt when he asked his question?
qa.a: Nitin was curious and a little puzzled, having seen that Amandeep wanted to be up there.

grounding: Shows a girl hurt that a rite is given only to boys, and a calm teacher explaining the tradition while listening and offering a way forward.

passage:
Before: When Dadi announced Divyansh's thread ceremony, Devika, nine, asked, "When is mine?" Dadi said, "Girls don't have it." Devika went quiet.
During: On the day, everyone crowded round Divyansh. He got new clothes, gifts and all the photos. Devika sat by the pillar with the sweets tray. When an aunty said, "Now he's grown up," Devika's eyes filled. She slipped away to the terrace.
After: That evening Dadi climbed up to the terrace, slowly. She sat beside Devika. "You're sad because it's only for boys." Devika nodded, crying. "That's fair to feel," Dadi said. "This ceremony is very old, from a time when only boys studied the scriptures. I was sad about it too when I was small." She took Devika's hand. "Tomorrow, you and I will read the Gita together, just us." Devika leaned against her.

qa.q: Where did Devika go when her eyes filled?
qa.a: She slipped away to the terrace.

qa.q: How did Devika feel when the aunty said "Now he's grown up"?
qa.a: She felt left out and hurt, her eyes filling with tears.

qa.q: What did Dadi do well on the terrace?
qa.a: She listened, named Devika's hurt as fair, explained the tradition's history calmly and offered her a shared reading of her own.

qa.q: How might Divyansh have experienced the day?
qa.a: Divyansh probably felt proud and the centre of attention, perhaps without noticing his sister was sad.

grounding: It illustrates a child who sees a rite given only to boys and feels left out, and a calm adult who explains the tradition while listening to her hurt.
